title: Care in the rule
hook: check-ups and help when needed: tie your camel and trust God, and Ben Sira's honor for the physician
tomorrow: a saint asked his own body to forgive him. what did he call it?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: rest. Antony said a bow always bent will break. Today, the help you've been putting off.

The reminder to book a check-up has been sitting in the inbox for weeks. It's possible to pray about a worry and still never call the doctor. A man once had a version of that question, about a camel. He'd left her outside, and before he went in, he asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: should I tie her up and trust in God? Or leave her loose and trust? It's a fair question, and the answer is short.
screen: `THE REMINDER, WEEKS OLD.` → `PRAY, AND NEVER CALL?` → `TIE THE CAMEL, OR TRUST?`

segments.voice: The answer, as the collection of Tirmidhi records it: tie her, and trust. Another hadith has desert Arabs asking whether they should seek medicine. Yes, he said, seek treatment, servants of God; God made no disease without making a remedy for it, except one: old age. That's tawakkul, trust in God, as Islam teaches it. Trust isn't leaving the rope on the ground. You tie the camel, take the medicine, book the appointment, and then trust God with what's beyond your hands. In this teaching, seeing a doctor isn't a lack of faith. It's part of it. Here's a neighbor who says something close. In the book of Sirach, the Jewish sage Ben Sira writes: honor the physician, for the Lord created him, and the Lord made medicines out of the earth, and the wise won't despise them. When you're sick, he says, pray, and then give the physician his place. The same two hands: prayer and the doctor. And one honest difference. The hadith goes straight to the remedy: there is one for every disease but old age, so seek it. Ben Sira puts prayer and turning from wrongdoing first, then gives the physician his place, and says the doctor prays too, for the treatment to go well. Care in your rule means both: the rope, and the trust.
screen: `TIE HER, AND TRUST.` · `EVERY DISEASE HAS A REMEDY, BUT AGE.` · `BEN SIRA: HONOR THE PHYSICIAN.` · `SEEK THE REMEDY; PRAY, THEN THE PHYSICIAN.` · then, large: `CARE.`

segments.voice: Think of one check-up you've been putting off: a doctor, a dentist, a counselor. Pick the day you'll call, and say it once out loud. Then sit with your hands loose for the rest of the time: the camel is tied, and the rest is trust.
Care in the rule: check-ups and help written into your rule, the camel tied and the trust kept.
Your line: care. Tie the camel, then trust; Ben Sira says honor the physician. Day 1651, rope tied.

screen: `DAY 1651 COUNTS.` → `THE BODY · 7 OF 8.` → `TOMORROW: A SAINT ASKED HIS OWN BODY TO FORGIVE HIM. WHAT DID HE CALL IT?`

howItsDone: Muslims describe seeking medicine as part of tawakkul, trust in God, and Jewish and Christian readers of Sirach honor physicians as God's gift; people on other paths pray and see a doctor too. A personal rule can name regular check-ups.

Tirmidhi.meaning: a scholar whose collection of hadith is widely used

hadith.meaning: a report of the Prophet Muhammad's words or deeds

tawakkul.meaning: trust in God, after doing your part

Sirach.meaning: a book of Jewish wisdom, in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles

Ben Sira.meaning: the Jewish sage who wrote the book of Sirach

sources.ref: Jami at-Tirmidhi 2517 (the man asks whether to tie his camel and trust, or leave it loose and trust: 'tie it and trust')
Sunan Abu Dawud 3855 (seek treatment; God has not made a disease without a remedy, except old age)
Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 38:1-14 (honor the physician; the Lord created medicines out of the earth; pray, then give place to the physician; physicians also pray)
